title: Kapoeta - Town, County and Geography Overview
content: Kapoeta is the administrative and commercial hub of Greater Kapoeta in Eastern Equatoria State, South Sudan, and the most important artisanal and small-scale gold mining district in the country. Kapoeta town lies on the east bank of the Singaita River at approximately 04 degrees 46 minutes 30 seconds North, 33 degrees 35 minutes 24 seconds East (4.775N, 33.59E), at an elevation of about 677 meters above sea level. It is roughly 275 kilometers by road east of Juba, the national capital, and about 240 kilometers from Torit, the state capital. The town was established as an administrative post in January 1927 by Captain Knollys, who reached the river that year. Kapoeta Airport is a dirt airstrip that links the area by air. The Lokichoggio-to-Juba road passes through the town, and the Nadapal-Lokichoggio border crossing into Kenya is the main artery for gold smuggling. The 2008 census recorded about 7,000 people in Kapoeta town, with the Toposa the dominant ethnic group alongside the Didinga, Murle, Boya, and Jie. Greater Kapoeta comprises the counties of Kapoeta North, Kapoeta South, and Kapoeta East, plus Budi County which is administratively separate but geologically and economically part of the same gold district. The area is a semi-arid rangeland of clay soil dotted with short, thorny shrubs, with distinct wet and dry seasons and frequent droughts and cattle raids. Kapoeta has long been known as a gold area, with mining activity documented since at least the 1950s.

title: Kapoeta Claim Coordinates - UTM 36N and Decimal Degrees
content: Target claim area coordinates within the Greater Kapoeta gold district, Eastern Equatoria State, South Sudan, referenced to UTM zone 36N (WGS84 datum). LEFT BOUNDARY CORNER: UTM 36N Easting 540003, Northing 492860, which converts to approximately 4.458881 degrees North, 33.360579 degrees East. RIGHT BOUNDARY CORNER: UTM 36N Easting 539515, Northing 492768, which converts to approximately 4.458051 degrees North, 33.356179 degrees East. These two corners define a small concession block spanning roughly 488 meters east-west (540003 minus 539515) and about 92 meters north-south (492860 minus 492768), i.e. a compact parcel of roughly 0.05 square kilometers (about 5 hectares). The claim center lies near 4.4585N, 33.3584E. Note that this location sits approximately 35 kilometers southwest of Kapoeta town center (4.775N, 33.59E), on the drier south-western flank of the district toward the Toposa plains. For reference, the Singaita River passes through Kapoeta town at 4.772644N, 33.584132E, and near town the river is about 150 yards wide with a normally sandy dry bed that can flood rapidly after heavy rainstorms in the Didinga Hills. The claim area is within the Karasuk Supergroup terrane, whose western margin is bounded by reworked Neoproterozoic rocks of the Sahara Metacraton. UTM zone 36N central meridian is 33 degrees East. Local grid, geological, and licensing coordinates should always be re-verified against the official concession title, Ministry of Mining records, and a GPS survey on the ground before any operational decision.

title: Kapoeta Gold - Full Historical Record (Colonial Era to Present)
content: GOLD HISTORY OF KAPOETA, EASTERN EQUATORIA. COLONIAL ERA (1899-1956): Kapoeta lay inside the Anglo-Egyptian Sudan's Equatoria Province. The first recorded administrative contact was Captain Knollys, who established the Kapoeta post on the east bank of the Singaita River in January 1927. Colonial administrators and geologists documented gold showings in the region from the early decades of the 20th century; the Karasuk Supergroup sequence on the border zone between Sudan, Uganda and Kenya was mapped through the 1920s-1960s. The Toposa herders who dominated the area knew of gold and placer workings long before the colonial era. POST-INDEPENDENCE SUDAN (1956-1983): Radio Tamazuj's interview with the mining ministry confirms that 'even right from the 1950s, Kapoeta was known to be a gold area in Eastern Equatoria State'. Exploration remained largely geological reconnaissance. SYSTEMATIC SURVEYS (1970s-1980s): Hunting Technical Services Ltd carried out regional geological and mineral surveys in the 1970s (1976, 1980) across Southern Sudan, mapping the Karasuk Supergroup, marble belts near Kapoeta, and alluvial gold showings. The Belgian Geological Survey and Belgian Mining Exploration Mission worked in the region in 1983 and 1985, identifying and documenting specific placer gold sites. These surveys noted alluvial gold grades on the order of 0.3-1.5 g per cubic meter in river gravels, with garnet, magnetite, and ilmenite as the associated heavy minerals. The Hunting survey of 1980 also highlighted hydrothermal alteration zones with silicified quartz veins, sericite and pyrite east and southeast of Kapoeta. CIVIL WAR ERA (1983-2005): The Second Sudanese Civil War froze most formal exploration. Kapoeta changed hands between the SPLA and government forces; the area suffered cattle raiding, displacement, and landmine contamination. Artisanal panning continued informally. POST-CPA AND INDEPENDENCE (2005-2018): After the 2005 Comprehensive Peace Agreement and independence in July 2011, foreign companies re-entered. New Kush Exploration and Equator Gold were the first two national companies to begin gold operations in Kapoeta before the 2012 Mining Act. The South Sudan Mining Act 2012 established the legal framework for prospecting, exploration, development, and artisanal and small-scale mining licenses. GOLD RUSH (2019-2022): A major gold rush drew tens of thousands of miners. The government suspended operation licenses of mining companies in late 2019 to stop illegal operations, halting industrial-style work. In 2020, the Enough Project reported the criminalization of the Kapoeta gold sector, and the Bank of South Sudan announced plans to purchase crude gold locally, focusing on Kapoeta. Eye Radio (August 2021) documented sites at Nakeke and Faka in Kapoeta South, Chinese-owned Shino Minerals (a well-established Chinese company with a track record in Bushenyi, western Uganda) operating along the Singaita River, a deadly hole collapse at Faka in early February 2021 that killed three, and abandoned excavators across the district. 2022-2026: Formal mining remained mostly exploration-stage. ASWA Mining Company was contracted by the government in March 2023 to carry out mineral exploration. Companies reported at Greater Kapoeta include New Kush Exploration, Natura (Turkish), Blackstone (South Sudanese), Equator Gold Ltd, Gold Leaf Ltd, and Australian NUCO, whose license was terminated for violating concession terms. Governor Louis Lobong Lojore suspended operations at Nakere in Kapoeta South in June 2026 over community unrest and environmental complaints. Gold extraction expanded to Lauro Payam and Maji Boma in Budi County in 2023 with machinery.

title: Kapoeta Geology - Karasuk Supergroup Lithology and Structure
content: GEOLOGY OF THE KAPOETA GOLD DISTRICT. TECTONIC SETTING: The Kapoeta area lies within the Karasuk Supergroup, a Neoproterozoic mobile belt situated between the Archaean basement to the west and the East African Orogen to the east, within the Arabian-Nubian Shield context of the East African Orogeny (Pan-African). In Kapoeta the Karasuk Supergroup occupies a broad belt roughly 40 km wide east to west, covering the eastern extremity of South Sudan and extending as far north as Daga Post in Upper Nile (Hunting, 1976). It is limited to the west and east by reworked Neoproterozoic rocks of the Sahara Metacraton and by extrusive basic and acidic volcanic rocks respectively. The belt continues south into Karamoja in northeastern Uganda. METAMORPHISM: Most Karasuk Supergroup rocks were metamorphosed to amphibolite facies (Almond, 1969), while the metasediments are of greenschist facies regional metamorphism. In the Sekerr area the sequence is an imbricate zone with strong thrusting, and the relationship is less well understood at the northern end of the belt around Kapoeta (Vail, 1988). STRATIGRAPHY AND LITHOLOGIES: The Karasuk Supergroup in the area is an assemblage of metamorphosed igneous and sedimentary rocks including andesite, basalts, amphibolites, biotite-hornblende gneisses, marbles, quartzites, chlorite, garnet and graphite schists, altered granites, alaskites, ultrabasic rocks, and gabbros. Metavolcanics (metabasalt, meta-andesite, meta-rhyolite) are exposed around Buno stream on the Kapoeta-Narus road. Two types of marble exist: a low-lying marble near the police post invaded by minute quartz veinlets, and a second occurrence east at Napotpot and Kawokono associated with quartzo-feldspathic gneisses and intruded by alaskites, including the Kawokono bull's-eye structure area with grey banded and white marble. STRUCTURE: Field observations show the metavolcano-sedimentary rocks strike NW-SE, NNW-SSE, N-S, and N10E in places, with vertical to sub-vertical dips, the dip direction varying NE to SW. Remote sensing and field mapping identified four main structural trends: N-S, NNW-SSE, NW-SE, and NE-SW. The N-S and NNW-SSE trends are the potential controls on mineralization. Vein systems include NW-SE-trending quartz veins impregnated with sulphides, pyrite, and chalcopyrite, for example around Moruarangani. The metavolcano-sedimentary assemblages in the area are tilted to near-vertical dip with a general NW-SE strike orientation. Overburden masks most of the Neoproterozoic juvenile metavolcano-sedimentary sequences, and vegetation cover affects mapping around the Didinga Hills and Dongotona mountains.

title: Kapoeta Gold Mineralization Style and Geochemistry
content: GOLD MINERALIZATION AT KAPOETA. DEPOSIT TYPE: The alluvial gold deposits of Kapoeta are hosted in metavolcano-sedimentary sequences and in vein-type (lode) deposits. The mineralization is orogenic in nature with a strong epigenetic character, although a syngenetic origin cannot be ruled out (Bali, University of the Witwatersrand MSc, 2023). The deposit model is an orogenic gold system associated with regional shear zones that bound the greenstone belt. HOST LITHOLOGIES: The host lithologies may vary from quartz veins to schists, amphibolites, quartzo-feldspathic gneisses, and ultramafics, plus the marbles, all related to the N-S, NNW-SSE and NW-SE trending shear zones that limit the greenstone belt. Vein indicators include NW-SE-trending quartz veins impregnated with sulphides, pyrite, and chalcopyrite around Moruarangani. GEOCHEMISTRY: Whole-rock geochemistry plotted on the TAS discrimination diagrams shows the rocks analysed are dominantly tholeiitic with minor calc-alkaline units. Trace elements normalized to primitive mantle show low concentrations of Zr, Hf, Nb and Ta. Chondrite-normalized REE values indicate general enrichment of LREE relative to HREE with a negative Eu anomaly. On tectonic discrimination diagrams the rocks of Greater Kapoeta belong to a marine environment related to a spreading centre, oceanic island, oceanic ridge, and oceanic floor. PATHFINDER ELEMENTS: The distribution of Cu, Co, Cr and Ni, and their high concentrations in the geochemical anomaly maps, suggest these elements are the potential pathfinders for gold in the area. Gold occurrence and anomaly mapping combined with structural mapping shows that N-S and NNW-SSE trends are the potential controls on mineralization. MARBLE AND GOLD ASSOCIATION: Marble rocks near Kapoeta are associated with gold mineralization; the extensive marble/limestone occurrences near Kapoeta were studied in the 1970s with a view to establishing a cement industry, plans that were interrupted by the wars. SECONDARY (PLACER) GEOCHEMISTRY: Alluvial placer gold in the district is associated with heavy mineral suites of garnet, magnetite, and ilmenite, indicating derivation from amphibolite-facies metasediments and metavolcanics. Copper-gold correlation is typical of the wider region: the Hofrat Ennahas copper-gold deposit in Western Bahr el Ghazal assays 1-5% Cu and up to 3 g Au/t, showing the regional gold-copper association. For exploration, stream-sediment panning, soil geochemistry on Cu/Co/Cr/Ni, and mapping of quartz-sulphide veins along N-S to NNW-SSE shear zones are the recommended targeting methods.

title: Kapoeta Satellite Imagery and Remote Sensing Guide
content: SATELLITE IMAGERY AND REMOTE SENSING FOR THE KAPOETA DISTRICT. PROVEN DATASETS: Landsat-8 Operational Land Imager (OLI) and SRTM-DEM (Shuttle Radar Topography Mission) satellite images were successfully employed in the Kapoeta area by Francis Bali (University of the Witwatersrand MSc, 2023) to map lithological units, highlight hydrothermal alteration, and outline structural trends. Landsat-7 ETM+ and SRTM data were also used in the earlier phases of that study. These datasets are free to download from USGS EarthExplorer, and are appropriate for a district-scale exploration program over the claim area. IMAGE PROCESSING TECHNIQUES: Band ratio and principal component analyses on Landsat-8 OLI data were effective in mapping lithological units and major structural trends. Hydrothermal alteration mapping is challenging in Kapoeta because overburden masks most of the Neoproterozoic juvenile metavolcano-sedimentary sequences, and vegetation cover affects mapping around the Didinga Hills and Dongotona mountains. PRACTICAL BAND RATIOS (Landsat): Band ratio B4/B2 highlights the presence of ferric oxides (ilmenites, hematite) from intense surface oxidation, widespread in the artisanal mining areas which are restricted to weathered or altered metasediments. Band ratio B6/B7 refers to clay minerals, of which kaolinites are the most abundant in the area. Lighter-toned pixels in the ratio imagery coincide with hydrothermal alteration zones characterized by silicification, quartz veins, sericite, and pyrite (Hunting Geology and Geophysics Ltd, 1980). Areas east and southeast of Kapoeta are known artisanal gold mining sites and appear as altered, iron-oxide rich zones. STRUCTURAL MAPPING: SRTM-DEM and OLI panchromatic data were used to extract lineaments; four main trends were identified: N-S, NNW-SSE, NW-SE, and NE-SW. The N-S and NNW-SSE trends are the potential controls on mineralization and should be targeted for structural mapping of the claim. RECOMMENDED WORKFLOW FOR THE CLAIM AREA: (1) Download Landsat-8/9 OLI Level-2 surface reflectance and SRTM 1-arc DEM for the tile covering 4.4-4.5N, 33.2-33.5E. (2) Run band ratios B4/B2 (iron oxide) and B6/B7 (clay/kaolinite), plus a PCA and false-color composites. (3) Extract lineaments from the DEM and map N-S and NNW-SSE trends crossing the claim. (4) Combine alteration anomaly maps with the claim footprint (UTM 36N, E 539515-540003, N 492768-492860) to prioritize field targets. (5) Follow up with Sentinel-2 MSI at 10 m resolution for higher detail, and drone photogrammetry for site-scale mapping.

title: Kapoeta Alluvial and Placer Gold Deposits
content: ALLUVIAL AND PLACER GOLD IN THE KAPOETA DISTRICT. GENERAL: The placer (secondary) gold deposits of Kapoeta are the principal source of the district's production and are mined by artisanal panning in seasonal streams and river gravels. They are derived from erosion of the Karasuk Supergroup metavolcano-sedimentary host rocks and quartz-sulphide vein systems, and are transported and concentrated in stream sediments and floodplain gravels. GRADES: Historical and survey data indicate alluvial gold grades on the order of 0.3-1.5 g per cubic meter in river gravels (Hunting Technical Services, 1976). Regional heavy mineral suites include garnet, magnetite, and ilmenite, useful as indicators when panning. KNOWN WORKINGS: Sites documented by NGOs and media include Nakeke (about a 30-minute drive from Kapoeta town, where men dig pits and women and children pan in the waters of the Singaita River), Faka in the Ngauro area (a roughly 1 square km area opened up by a 'Chinese' company using excavators, now flooded and forming a lake that cuts off Ngauro town from Faka in the rains), Nanaknak (also spelled Anak-anak or Naknak), Napotpot (garnet schists overlain by an ultramafic body), Nakapelichor, Namurnyang/Namurungang, Lauro (Didinga Hills), Buno stream on the Kapoeta-Narus road, Kokumai, Natartar, Nitemoar and Morungapi in Kapoeta East, and Moruarangani with NW-SE trending quartz-sulphide veins. DRAINAGE: The Singaita River (also Khawr/ Rigl Thingaita) flows through Kapoeta town; near the town it is about 150 yards wide with a sandy dry bed that can become a raging flood after heavy storms in the Didinga Hills. A 125-meter drift was built to cross the Singaita at Kapoeta with USAID funding in 1983. The Nathilani River is a tributary. The claim area at UTM 36N 539515-540003 E, 492768-492860 N lies on the southwestern flank of the district, within the same drainage basin toward the Toposa plains, where seasonal wadis transport sediment from the Karasuk terrane. TECHNIQUE: Recovery is by digging pits into gravel and weathered zones, then panning the soil and gravel in water to recover fine gold particles. Average output per miner is small (less than 0.5 grams per miner per day on average), which makes the trade dependent on aggregation by buyers. RECOMMENDATIONS: For the claim, conduct bulk stream-sediment panning along active wadi channels and terrace gravels, quantify gold grain size and shape (flattened/rough grains imply proximal versus distal source), sample heavy mineral concentrates for garnet-magnetite-ilmenite ratios, and trace indicator suites upstream to locate the primary lode source.

title: Kapoeta Artisanal Mining, Production Estimates and Gold Economy
content: ARTISANAL MINING AND THE GOLD ECONOMY OF KAPOETA. SCALE: Estimates put the number of miners in the Greater Kapoeta area at about 60,000, working at roughly 80 different locations, including Nanaknak, Lauro (Didinga Hills), Napotpot, and Namurnyang (Enough Project, 2020). Other estimates for Kapoeta alone range around 10,000 miners, fluctuating seasonally and with security conditions (GI-TOC, 2023). Over 30 companies operate in legal exploration and illegal mining across Kapoeta, with more than 70 concessions granted. PRODUCTION: There are no official production statistics; neither the Ministry of Mining nor the Ministry of Trade has data on gold production or trade. Estimates of total South Sudan gold production range from 1-2 tonnes per month (Enough Project, 2020), to roughly 5 tonnes per year (SWISSAID estimate, based on an IMF/World Bank figure of USD 270 million of gold smuggled out in 2022, USD 150 million to Uganda and USD 120 million to Dubai), to over 22 tonnes per year if extrapolated from a World Bank figure of 1 gram per miner per day for 60,000 miners. SWISSAID considers 5 tonnes per year the most plausible figure. The Kapoeta government purchases roughly 10 kilograms (about 322 troy ounces) of gold per month from local miners, but only about 1 kilogram reaches the Bank of South Sudan annually. TRADE AND SMUGGLING: The gold trade is dominated by Somali, Ugandan, Kenyan, and Chinese buyers. Gold moves from mining sites to Kapoeta town via intermediaries (one buyer aggregates an entire mining group's gold), then to Juba, or to Nairobi via the Nadapal-Lokichoggio border and Eastleigh, Kakuma and refugee camps, to Kampala via Liria/Juba/Nimule, or to Dubai. One smuggler reported transporting up to 15 kilograms by road to Nairobi per month. Traders estimate unauthorized traders manage 1-2 tonnes per month. Prices at mining sites were as low as 70% of international spot price in March 2022, well below East African peers, because miners cannot negotiate and sell to aggregators. In 2020 the Bank of South Sudan announced plans to purchase crude gold locally with Kapoeta as the focus, but in practice only about 1 kg per year reached the central bank. PRICES AND CURRENCY: The unstable exchange rate of the US dollar against the South Sudanese pound forces miners and traders to smuggle to Nairobi or Kampala; payments are often received via M-Pesa. REGULATION: The Mining Act 2012 governs the sector; artisanal mining requires registration with the Ministry of Mining, and only South Sudanese citizens may hold licenses, but enforcement is weak. IMPLICATIONS FOR THE CLAIM: Any operation must plan for high security risk, informal local governance, community expectations, and gold sales at a significant discount to spot unless a formal offtake channel is secured.

title: Kapoeta Mining Companies and Concessions
content: COMPANIES AND CONCESSIONS AT KAPOETA, EASTERN EQUATORIA. NATIONAL COMPANIES: New Kush Exploration and Equator Gold Ltd were the first two national companies to begin gold operations in Kapoeta and Luri before the 2012 Mining Act. Blackstone is a South Sudanese company registered to explore gold in Kapoeta. Gold Leaf Ltd also operates in Eastern Equatoria. ASWA Mining Company was contracted by the government in March 2023 to carry out mineral exploration in Greater Kapoeta. FOREIGN COMPANIES: Natura is a Turkish company with five concessions, doing exploration work. Al-Cardinal, a Sudanese company owned by businessman Ashraf Seed Ahmed Hussein Ali (under Global Magnitsky sanctions since October 2019), reportedly holds the greatest number of licenses (six concessions) nationally. Manaji, a United Arab Emirates company, holds four concessions. Other companies reported in the sector include Zungao of China, Sky Gold of Lebanon, AG Vision of Nigeria, and 4MB of the USA, each with one concession, plus two South African companies, Australian Epic (four concessions), and two Sudanese companies (eight concessions). NUCO Mining Ltd, an Australian company, was awarded an exploration license in Kapoeta but had it revoked for deviating from traditional exploration methods (concession terms). Shino Minerals, a Chinese company with a track record in Bushenyi, western Uganda, operated along the Singaita River at Kapoeta with about 20 laborers including Ugandans, using excavators, until the government suspended gold mining licenses in late 2019. Local people refer to several operators simply as 'Chinese' companies. At Nakere in Kapoeta South, Nakere Gold Mining Company, Eastern Equatoria Mining Corporation, and Prudential Holdings operate, and Governor Louis Lobong Lojore ordered the temporary suspension of mining operations there in June 2026 amid community unrest and complaints over environmental damage and inadequate local benefits. An Israeli company, Duar, is being partnered with to support local mining. LICENSING CONTEXT: Companies must be controlled by South Sudanese individuals to obtain mining licenses under the 2012 Mining Act. The Ministry of Mining has revoked licenses of companies with insufficient financial capacity; among 41 active companies are ASWA Mining Ltd, New Kush Exploration, and Gold Leaf Ltd in Eastern Equatoria. Political economy: politically exposed persons, including relatives of senior officials, have held shares in at least 32 South Sudanese mining companies (The Sentry, 2020); some 200 individuals work unofficially as gold traders in Greater Equatoria. Compliance on the claim area requires verifying the concession holder, title chain, and community agreements before operating.

title: Kapoeta Security, Community, Environmental and Operational Risks
content: SECURITY, COMMUNITY, ENVIRONMENTAL AND OPERATIONAL RISKS AT KAPOETA. SECURITY: Eastern Equatoria has experienced armed cattle raiding, inter-communal violence, and low-intensity conflict over land and resources. Gold mining has increased militarization: the military holds interests in exploration licenses, opposition groups informally control artisanal mining sites, and conflict between the Didinga and Toposa over gold was documented (ISRP, 2025). In February 2023, at least seven people, including a woman and two children, were killed in a resource conflict in Budi County. An armed raid on a Kapoeta security office in 2025 left five officers critically injured. Landmines and unexploded ordnance from the civil wars remain in parts of the district. Unregistered companies, some with ties to influential individuals, are involved in illegal extraction; the Enough Project (2020) described the sector as criminalized, ungoverned, and poorly regulated, with kleptocratic networks controlling the trade. COMMUNITY: Mining companies that fail to honor agreements face conflict with communities. Communities in Ngauro demand that companies build roads, schools, and hospitals; companies have been accused of extracting gold and leaving without delivering promised development. An operation at Kapoeta must sign and honor a formal community development agreement with the Toposa and Didinga communities and their traditional authorities before work begins. SAFETY: Artisanal pits are dangerous: at Faka (Ngaulo area) three miners died in February 2021 when a more than 10-meter-deep hole collapsed; three others survived. Pits at Nakeke reach nearly 20 meters deep without support. Environmentalists have documented at least ten deaths related to environmental damage caused by gold mining in Greater Kapoeta. ENVIRONMENT: Large tracts of land in Ngauro and Nakeke have lost vegetation cover; abandoned pits and trenches are not reclaimed, causing massive gullies, excessive run-off, heavy erosion, reduced soil infiltration, reduced groundwater recharge, and loss of land productivity. At Faka, a flooded abandoned excavation about 1 km square cuts off communities in the rains. Water bodies are contaminated. OPERATIONAL: There is no industrial mining yet in South Sudan; formal operations are exploration-stage. Only South Sudanese citizens may hold licenses. Infrastructure is limited: dry-season-only roads, no rail, intermittent fuel, no power grid (diesel generators only), and a dirt airstrip at Kapoeta. Currency instability (South Sudanese pound) and the black-market discount on gold (down to 70% of spot) are financial risks. RECOMMENDATIONS: Secure a verified legal title; sign community agreements; hire locally including armed escort planning; ensure pit support and slope safety; conduct baseline environmental assessment; and establish a traceable offtake channel to avoid smuggling discount risk.

title: Kapoeta Infrastructure, Access, Climate and Logistics
content: INFRASTRUCTURE, ACCESS, CLIMATE AND LOGISTICS FOR KAPOETA. ACCESS: Kapoeta town is about 275 km by road east of Juba and roughly 240 km from Torit. The Lokichoggio-to-Juba road passes through the town and connects to Kenya via the Nadapal-Lokichoggio border post. Roads in the district are dry-season only; heavy rains cut communities off and the Singaita River floods rapidly after storms in the Didinga Hills. A 125-meter drift crosses the Singaita River at Kapoeta, built with USAID funding in 1983. The claim area (UTM 36N, E 539515-540003, N 492768-492860) lies roughly 35 km southwest of Kapoeta town on the Toposa plains, reachable by track. AIR: Kapoeta Airport is a dirt airstrip that supports light aircraft, useful for crew rotation and urgent logistics; Juba International Airport is the main entry point from Nairobi, Entebbe, Addis Ababa, and Cairo. POWER AND FUEL: There is no national power grid; operations rely on diesel generators. Fuel is trucked in from Juba or Kenya and is subject to price volatility. WATER: The Singaita River and its tributaries provide seasonal water; dry-season water is drawn from wells and holes dug in river beds. Potable water treatment is required for camps. CLIMATE: The district is semi-arid with two distinct seasons: wet (approximately May-November, peaking with heavy storms) and dry (December-April). Annual rainfall is low and erratic; droughts are recurrent and drive pastoralists and farmers toward mining as an alternative livelihood. DAY-TO-DAY OPERATIONS: Banking is limited; gold is often traded in cash and M-Pesa. Food, medical, and security supplies are scarce locally and must be planned. The nearest sophisticated mining services and assay laboratories are in Juba, Nairobi, or Kampala; local assay capacity is absent, so samples must be flown or driven out. COMMUNICATIONS: Mobile coverage exists around Kapoeta town but is unreliable in the bush; satellite communication (e.g., satellite phones or Starlink) is recommended for field teams. LOGISTICAL PLAN: Use Kapoeta airstrip for priority cargo and personnel; pre-position fuel and spares before the wet season; schedule field work on the claim in the dry season (December-April); and maintain a staged resupply route via Juba or Lokichoggio. SECURITY NOTE: Movement on remote tracks carries cattle-raiding and armed-group risk; coordinate with local authorities and the community, and consider armed escort for convoys.

title: Kapoeta Data Sources and Bibliography
content: DATA SOURCES AND BIBLIOGRAPHY FOR THE KAPOETA GOLD DISTRICT. PRIMARY ACADEMIC SOURCE: Bali, Francis Khamis Alex (2023). 'Potential Source for the Alluvial Gold Deposit in the Kapoeta Area, Eastern Equatoria State, South Sudan', MSc dissertation, University of the Witwatersrand, Johannesburg, https://hdl.handle.net/10539/41961; preprint 'Integrated Remote Sensing Techniques and Field Investigation in Identification of Potential Sources for Alluvial Gold Deposit in Kapoeta', DOI 10.21203/rs.3.rs-10378546/v1. This study used Landsat-8 OLI and SRTM-DEM, geochemical anomaly mapping (Cu, Co, Cr, Ni), and field investigation, concluding the gold is orogenic with epigenetic character, hosted in metavolcano-sedimentary sequences and vein-type deposits. GOVERNMENT AND NGO REPORTS: Enough Project (2020), 'The Criminalization of South Sudan's Gold Sector: Kleptocratic Networks and the Gold Trade in Kapoeta', enoughproject.org. The Sentry (2020), 'Untapped and Unprepared'. Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (2023), 'Tarnished Hope: Crime and Corruption in South Sudan's Gold Sector'. SWISSAID African Gold Report (2025), 'South Sudan'. ISPR-SS (2025), 'Illicit Mining and Revenue Collection Risks in South Sudan's Gold Concentrate Sector'. WORLD BANK AND IMF: World Bank (2022) on South Sudan's oil-dependent economy; IMF/World Bank figure of USD 270 million of gold smuggled from South Sudan in 2022. GEOLOGICAL SURVEYS: Hunting Technical Services Ltd (1976, 1980) regional geological and mineral surveys of Southern Sudan; Belgian Geological Survey and Belgian Mining Exploration Mission (1983, 1985) placer gold studies at Kapoeta; Vail, J.R. (1988) on the East African belt around Kapoeta; Almond (1969) on Karasuk metamorphism; Vearncombe (1983) on the Sekerr imbricate zone; Westerhof et al. (2014); Kujjo, Cosmas Pitia (2019), 'Mineral Exploration and Sustainable Development: A Case Study in the Republic of South Sudan', University of Kentucky, DOI 10.13023/etd.2019.061. MEDIA: Eye Radio (2021-08-24), 'Taking from the poor: A mirror into South Sudan's gold-mining business', Ayuen Panchol; Radio Tamazuj (2021-06-07), interview with mining ministry; The Radio Community (2023-07-10), Governor Lobong on ASWA exploration; Sudans Post (2026-06-27), Nakere suspension; InfoNile (2024-10-12), 'South Sudan's Gold Rush'; tndNews Uganda (2024-08-29), 'Kapoeta's gold rush'. GENERAL REFERENCES: Wikipedia 'Kapoeta' and 'Singaita River' articles; Leonardi, C. (2005), 'Violence, Law and Civil Power in the Anglo-Egyptian Sudan: Colonial Governance in Southern Sudan 1900-1956', Durham University PhD; African Studies Center, Michigan State University (1981), Northeast African Studies Vol 3. NOTE: Production figures for South Sudan gold are unofficial estimates only; no official national production or trade statistics exist.
